title: Timing-only CAN detectors miss masquerades, and their labels hide half the truth
problem: Vehicle intrusion detectors are often judged on published benchmarks, but a benchmark's attack set, alert rule and labels decide what its scores mean.
mechanism: [KNOWN: code inspection at e0c862d] ORNL's benchmark learns each CAN ID's normal inter-arrival time and flags frames that arrive too soon, using Mean, Binning, Gaussian or KDE rules. Mean uses a 3-of-last-6 rule, while Gaussian and KDE require 3 consecutive flags. Labels mark every frame of the target ID inside the injection window, regardless of payload. Masquerade and accelerator captures are excluded as out of scope.
finding: [KNOWN: recorded experiment, 2026-11-15] On the public ROAD dataset, an independent re-implementation reproduced the published Mean and Binning confusion matrices exactly. Mean and Binning had recall 0 on all 13 masquerade captures. Gaussian caught most of one masquerade whose injector runs about 14% slow, at precision 0.32 or lower. Switching Gaussian to the 3-of-6 rule raised its best F1 from 0.26 to 0.92. Payload-based labels kept exactly 50.00% of published positives in every targeted log, and F1 at the published optima fell to about 0.65. These results come from offline replay of one vehicle's dynamometer captures.

experiment.limitations: Independent re-implementation, checked against the pinned helper code on small inputs; the notebook itself was not run. Python 3.10.20 with numpy 1.23.5, pandas 1.5.3, scipy 1.9.3 and scikit-learn 1.1.3 on macOS arm64. Requires the ROAD dataset (not committed). Offline replay of one vehicle's dynamometer captures; says nothing about live vehicles or the paper's Raspberry Pi plug-in. KDE was skipped. The referee could not prove the predictions were written before the results.

adaptation: [INFERRED] When evaluating or building a CAN IDS, report masquerade results separately, label by payload rather than by ID inside a window, and treat the alert-sufficiency rule as a tunable component. A one-sided slow-period or period-drift test is a candidate for the masquerades that change timing slightly; it remains untested.
unknowns: Whether a period-drift test catches the coolant-style masquerades at a false-positive rate of 1e-3 or less is untested.
Behavior on other vehicles, live buses or ORNL's plug-in prototype is unknown.
Whether the ID-window labelling convention was a deliberate design choice is not stated in any source.
